trading model.def: A mathematical rule that takes inputs observed now, such as past prices or volumes, and produces a prediction of some quantity at a later time.

feature.def: One of the inputs to a model: a number known at the time the prediction is made, such as yesterday's return or today's volume.

target.def: The quantity a model is trained to predict, observed after the prediction is made, such as the next day's return or its direction.

prediction horizon.def: How far ahead a model predicts: the time between the moment its features are observed and the moment its target is measured.

regression model.def: A model that predicts a continuous quantity, such as a return, a price or a volatility.

classification model.def: A model that predicts which of a finite set of categories an outcome falls into, such as up or down, usually with a probability for each.

lookahead bias.def: The error of letting a backtest use information that was not available at the moment of the decision, such as a figure before its publication date. It makes a backtest look better than any real trader could have done.

overfitting.def: Fitting a model so closely to its training data that it captures the noise as well as the signal. An overfitted model looks excellent in sample and predicts poorly on new data.

bias-variance tradeoff.def: The balance between two sources of error in an estimate: bias, being consistently wrong in one direction, and variance, the noise that comes from a finite sample. Complex models cut bias and add variance.

signal-to-noise ratio.def: The size of the predictable part of a quantity relative to its unpredictable part. For short-horizon returns it is very small, so the signal is hard to tell from chance.

neural network.def: A flexible model built from many layers of weighted sums passed through simple nonlinear functions. It can have thousands or millions of parameters, which makes it prone to overfitting noisy data.

residual.def: The gap between what a model predicted and what actually happened, for one observation.

cross-validation.def: Testing a model by fitting it on part of the data and scoring it on a part it was not fitted to, rotating through the data. The standard k-fold version splits the data at random, which leaks the future into training when the data are a time series.

walk-forward analysis.def: Testing a model on time series by training it only on data before each test period and scoring it on that period, then moving forward and repeating.

purged k-fold cross-validation.def: A version of cross-validation for financial time series, described by López de Prado (2018), that removes from training any observations whose targets overlap the test period.

in-sample.def: Measured on the same data a model was fitted to. In-sample performance is optimistic, because the fit has partly adapted to that data's noise.

out-of-sample.def: Measured on data a model was not fitted to, such as a later period. It is the honest estimate of how the model would have performed in real time.

AR(1) model.def: An autoregressive model of order one: it predicts each period's value, such as a return, as a weight times the previous period's value plus a constant. The sign of the weight separates mean reversion from momentum.

innovation.def: The fresh random shock in each period of a time series model, unpredictable from anything that came before it.

mean reversion.def: The tendency of a move to be followed by a move in the opposite direction, so that prices drift back toward where they were. In a return series it shows as negative autocorrelation.

random walk.def: A series whose changes are independent of one another, so that the last move carries no information about the next.

efficient market hypothesis.def: The claim that prices already reflect available information. In its weakest form, past prices and returns cannot predict future returns.

stationary.def: Said of a time series whose statistical behavior, such as its mean and variance, stays the same over time rather than drifting or growing without limit.

autocorrelation.def: The correlation of a series with its own earlier values. The lag-1 autocorrelation of returns is the correlation between each period's return and the one before.

Hurst exponent.def: A number describing how the variance of cumulative returns grows with the horizon. It is 0.5 for a random walk, below 0.5 for a mean-reverting series and above 0.5 for a trending one.

variance ratio test.def: A test of the random-walk hypothesis from Lo and MacKinlay (1988) that compares the variance of multi-period returns with the one-period variance times the number of periods. A ratio above 1 indicates momentum, and below 1 mean reversion.

regime-switching model.def: A model with separate parameters for different market states, such as calm and stress, together with a rule or classifier that decides which state is active.

loss function.def: The measure of how badly a model's predictions miss the data, which fitting makes as small as possible. The usual choice is the mean squared error.

derivative.def: The slope of a curve at a point: how fast one quantity changes per unit change in another, for a very small change. At the lowest point of a smooth curve it is zero.

gradient.def: The list of slopes of a loss with respect to each of a model's parameters. It points in the direction in which the loss rises most steeply.

ordinary least squares.def: The standard way to fit a linear regression: the weights that minimize the sum of squared prediction errors, found exactly with a formula rather than by search.

gradient descent.def: A way to fit a model by repeatedly moving its parameters a small step downhill on the loss, in the direction opposite to the gradient.

learning rate.def: The step size in gradient descent: how far the parameters move for each unit of slope. Too large and the fit overshoots or diverges, too small and it crawls.

stochastic gradient descent.def: Gradient descent that computes each step's slope on a small random subset of the data, a mini-batch, so that it never needs all the data at once.

convex function.def: A function whose graph is bowl-shaped, so that the straight line between any two of its points lies on or above it. A convex loss has one minimum, which gradient descent finds from any start.

hyperparameter.def: A setting chosen before a model is fitted rather than learned from the data, such as the learning rate or the strength of a regularization penalty.

regularization.def: Adding a penalty for large parameter values to the loss a model minimizes, which shrinks the fitted weights and reduces overfitting.

ridge regression.def: Regression with a penalty on the sum of the squared weights, also called L2 regularization. It shrinks every weight toward zero but keeps them all.

lasso.def: Regression with a penalty on the sum of the absolute values of the weights, also called L1 regularization. It sets many weights exactly to zero, so it also selects features.

fractional Kelly.def: Sizing at a fixed fraction of the Kelly bet, usually a half or a quarter. It gives up some long-run growth for much shallower drawdowns and a buffer against an overestimated edge.

sizing function.def: A rule that turns the strength of a model's prediction into a position size, such as a constant size, a size proportional to the signal up to a cap, or a smooth curve that approaches the cap.
